old_entry.title: Super Mario RPG
old_entry.subtitle: When Mario Learns the Language of Role-Playing
old_entry.summary: Super Mario RPG brought Nintendo's characters into a role-playing adventure developed with Square.
body: Super Mario RPG brought Nintendo's characters into a role-playing adventure developed with Square. Released for Super Famicom in Japan in 1996, it sends Mario beyond the familiar rescue pattern after a new enemy takes over Bowser's castle. Towns, conversations and a travelling party give the journey a different scale.

Battles use commands, but a button pressed at the right moment can strengthen an attack or improve defence. This keeps a small physical action inside the turn-based structure. Choosing a move and carrying it out are connected, leaving room for both planning and practice.

Mallow and Geno join familiar figures including Bowser and Peach. Having a former enemy and the usual rescue target take roles in the party changes how Mario's world is encountered. The expanded cast gives battles different abilities while giving the adventure people to talk to, disagree with and rely on.

According to Yoshio Hongo of Nintendo, Super Mario RPG came out of Mario creator Shigeru Miyamoto's desire to make an RPG using Mario, as well as Square's desire to develop an RPG that could do better outside of Japan than their previous games. Development began in early 1994 after a business meeting between Nintendo and Square. The first phase was spent on deciding a basic system, while the isometric view was chosen to help bring the world to life. The game was originally conceived with weapons in mind, but as meetings with Miyamoto progressed, the development team realized that they did not fit with the Mario franchise, and left them out. An exception was the hammer, which Miyamoto insisted on keeping. One of the main concerns of the development team was they did not want to make a "normal RPG that simply substituted in Mario characters." To help the game fit with the Mario series, it was made to be more action- and movement-focused compared to Square's other RPGs, using concepts such as jumping and dashing. Development began in earnest during the second quarter of 1995, when the programming, story events, and graphics data were being implemented.

original.old_body: Super Mario RPG enters this calendar through concrete design choices rather than through anniversary alone. Recognizable elements such as Nintendo, Square, Mario connect collaboration across studios and disciplines with progression and role-playing systems. In 1996, those choices organize rules, production and presentation into an experience the player has to read while acting. That movement from intention to play is what makes the subject historically useful: systems, characters, technology and cultural context stop behaving like separate categories and begin to reinforce one another. The chapters that follow start from specific, verifiable details and trace their consequences, asking how Super Mario RPG established its identity and which parts of that identity continued to influence the medium afterward.

old_entry.title: Pokémon Red and Green
old_entry.subtitle: A collection designed to leave the screen
old_entry.summary: A link cable turned different copies of a portable game into a reason to meet.
body: Game Freak's Pokémon Red and Green launched in Japan in 1996. Capturing and developing creatures created a personal collection, while differences between versions encouraged players to trade through Game Boy's link cable.

Satoshi Tajiri's concept grew through a team whose work included Ken Sugimori's designs and Junichi Masuda's music and programming. The social exchange was not an extra attached to the adventure; it helped give the collection its meaning.

Pokémon Red and Green began the series on Game Boy in Japan in 1996. A player travels through a world of towns, routes and battles while catching and raising Pokémon. Choosing a version begins the journey, but it also leaves reasons to talk to someone who owns the other one.

Trading lets two players exchange Pokémon through a Game Link cable. Battles let them bring their trained teams into direct competition. The handheld's portability matters here: a collection can travel with its owner, then become something to compare and exchange face to face.

Differences between the versions and Pokémon that evolve through trading make exchange part of completing a collection. The connection is therefore more than an optional scoreboard. A design built around collecting creates a practical use for another player's cartridge, time and willingness to trade.

Pokémon Red Version and Pokémon Blue Version are popular 1996 role-playing video games (RPGs) developed by Game Freak and published by Nintendo for the Game Boy. They are the first installments of the Pokémon video game series and were first released in Japan as Pocket Monsters Red and Pocket Monsters Green, followed by the special edition Pocket Monsters Blue later that year. The games were released internationally in 1998 and 1999 as Pokémon Red and Pokémon Blue, while an enhanced version, Pokémon Yellow Version: Special Pikachu Edition, was released in Japan in 1998 and in other regions in 1999 and 2000.

The player controls the protagonist from an overhead perspective and navigates the fictional region of Kanto in a quest to master Pokémon battling. The goal is to become the Pokémon League Champion by defeating the eight Gym Leaders and the best Pokémon Trainers in the Kanto Region, the Elite Four. Another objective is to complete the Pokédex, an in-game encyclopedia, by obtaining all 151 Pokémon. Red and Blue use the Game Link Cable, which connects two Game Boy systems and allows Pokémon to be traded or battled between games. Both versions feature the same plot, and while they can be played separately, players must trade between both games to obtain all of the original 151 Pokémon.

Red and Blue were well-received, with critics praising the multiplayer options, especially the concept of trading. They received an aggregated score of 89% on GameRankings and are considered among the greatest games ever made, perennially ranked on top game lists including at least four years on IGN's "Top 100 Games of All Time". The games marked the beginning of a multibillion-dollar franchise, jointly selling over 400 million copies worldwide. The Red and Blue versions were remade for Game Boy Advance (and later the Nintendo Switch for the 30th anniversary) as FireRed and LeafGreen (2004) while Yellow was remade for Nintendo Switch as Let's Go, Pikachu! and Let's Go, Eevee! (2018). The originals were rereleased on the Virtual Console service for the Nintendo 3DS in 2016 to commemorate their twentieth anniversaries.

A team records more than tactical preferences. The creature caught on an early route can remain beside us through later cities, carrying the memory of where the journey began. Levels and nicknames make continuity visible, allowing a collection of species to become a personal account of travelling together.

The player begins in their hometown of Pallet Town in the Kanto Region (inspired by, but not to be confused with the real life Kantō region of Japan). After venturing alone into the tall grass, the player is stopped by Professor Samuel Oak, a famous Pokémon Researcher. Professor Oak explains to the player that wild Pokémon may be living there and encountering them alone can be very dangerous. He takes the player to his laboratory where the player meets Oak's grandson, a rival aspiring Pokémon Trainer. The player and the rival are both instructed to select a starter Pokémon for their travels out of Bulbasaur, Squirtle and Charmander. Oak's grandson will always choose the Pokémon which is stronger against the player's starting Pokémon. He will then challenge the player to a Pokémon battle with their newly obtained Pokémon and will continue to battle the player at certain points.

Midway through Red and Blue's development, lead designer Ken Sugimori felt that the game needed more "cute" Pokémon and was struggling to conceive of such designs. Attributing it to his male perspective, he brought in female Game Freak staff including Atsuko Nishida to join the development team. Tasked with developing the Pikachu species and its evolutionary line, she was given specific guidelines to work with, namely its role as an Electric-type Pokémon, that it evolved twice, and that the final evolution should "look strong". Pikachu evolves into Raichu through use of the game's "Thunderstone" item. Raichu was originally planned to evolve into a Pokémon species dubbed Gorochu, but this was cut due to cartridge space concerns. Later in the franchise, Sugimori would create a Pokémon that evolved into Pikachu named Pichu to complete the trinity. Nishida developed the original Pikachu sprites using a single color identity chosen to work within the Super Game Boy's hardware limitations. Afterwards, the design was finalized by Sugimori who, towards the end of development, drew the promotional art of all the species to give them a unified look and make any last-minute changes.

Masuda approaches each of his games with the mindset that a beginner should be able to easily play it. In view of this, his games begin in an easily approachable and accessible style, with more layers of complexity being introduced as the player progresses through the game. He believes that handheld systems provide an opportunity for social interaction that cannot be found on non-handheld console systems. He has stated that the continued use of 2D computer graphics has been integral to Pokémon's success.

old_entry.title: Inti Creates
old_entry.subtitle: Inti Creates and the Art of Making Classic 2D Feel Modern
old_entry.summary: Inti Creates was founded on May 8, 1996.
body: Inti Creates was founded on May 8, 1996. The studio would cross multiple hardware generations while preserving a specific expertise: translating the rhythm of 2D action into readable, responsive systems suited to different machines. From work on Mega Man Zero and ZX to original projects such as Azure Striker Gunvolt and Blaster Master Zero, its history shows that pixel art is not necessarily nostalgia. It can be a production and design choice able to evolve alongside controls, displays and audience expectations.

Inti Creates was established in Japan in 1996 and grew through projects where animation, collision and control response had to remain readable even on small screens. Specialization did not mean immobility. The studio learned to change resolutions, palettes, memory formats and input devices without losing one constant principle: action must communicate cause and effect immediately. That discipline made the team especially suited to series demanding strict rhythm and characters recognizable within only a few frames.

With Mega Man Zero, Inti Creates moved a home-console series into the constraints of Game Boy Advance. The smaller screen forced reconsideration of sprite size, danger distance and reading speed. The result emphasizes aggressive movement, close combat and sharp animation. Difficulty is not ornamental; it emerges from the density with which enemies, platforms and attacks enter the visible space. The studio therefore turns a hardware limitation into a faster, sharper identity.

Azure Striker Gunvolt shows how Inti Creates can begin with run-and-gun tradition and alter its logic. Players tag targets and use Gunvolt's electricity to damage them continuously while energy, mobility and risk interact. Shooting is no longer only a matter of pressing accurately at the right moment. It means building a temporary relationship between character and enemies. This changes combat rhythm and shows a studio interested in preserving 2D clarity without simply repeating systems from the past.

old_entry.summary: Donkey Kong Country 3: Dixie Kong's Double Trouble!  is a 1996 platform game developed by Rare and published by Nintendo for the Super Nintendo Entertainment System (SNES).
body: Donkey Kong Country 3: Dixie Kong's Double Trouble!  is a 1996 platform game developed by Rare and published by Nintendo for the Super Nintendo Entertainment System (SNES). It is the third installment of the Donkey Kong Country series, and serves as a sequel to 1995's Donkey Kong Country 2: Diddy's Kong Quest. It was also re-released for the Game Boy Advance (GBA) in 2005. The game was made available to download on the Wii's Virtual Console service in 2007, as well as for the Wii U's Virtual Console in 2014.

The plot centers on Dixie Kong and her cousin, Kiddy Kong, in their attempts to save the captured Donkey Kong and Diddy Kong from the series' villain King K. Rool. The game is set in the "Northern Kremisphere", a fictionalized version of northern Europe and Canada. Dixie Kong's Double Trouble! utilises the same Silicon Graphics technology from its predecessors, which features the use of pre-rendered 3D imagery. The game received positive reviews upon release; critics praised the visuals and various aspects of gameplay, but noted a lack of innovation.

old_entry.title: Fire Emblem: Genealogy of the Holy War
old_entry.subtitle: Fire Emblem Turns a War into Inheritance
old_entry.summary: Nintendo released Fire Emblem: Genealogy of the Holy War for Super Famicom in Japan on May 14, 1996.
body: Nintendo released Fire Emblem: Genealogy of the Holy War for Super Famicom in Japan on May 14, 1996. Intelligent Systems expanded map scale and built the campaign around two generations of characters. Relationships, marriages and inheritance are not only narrative elements. They determine who will fight in the second half and which abilities may be passed down. The game therefore connects genealogy and strategy, making the passage of time visible in the rules. A personal bond can become a military consequence many chapters later.

Genealogy of the Holy War uses maps much larger than many earlier entries in the series. Castles, roads and groups of units form fronts that can require long movement, and capturing a position changes the flow of battle. Scale creates a political feeling: the player is not clearing one room or isolated fortress but crossing entire regions. Cavalry, formation and movement planning therefore matter more. Terrain is not only a tactical obstacle; it becomes a visible measure of the war being told.

Relationships among first-generation characters can lead to the children who fight in the second half. Equipment, statistics and skills are influenced by parents, turning personal affinity into strategic planning. The system makes the future a constant presence. Choosing who fights near whom is not only about the current turn because it can alter a team that does not yet exist. Fire Emblem therefore joins melodrama and optimization without separating them: emotional attachment and calculation share the same mechanism.

The two-generation structure allows the game to make a narrative rupture unusual for the series at the time. After investing time, equipment and affection in the first army, the player must reinterpret the world through children and the consequences left by their parents. The rules remain recognizable, but their emotional meaning changes. An inherited weapon or transmitted trait functions as concrete memory. The genealogy system therefore makes the history of the war persist inside the numbers used to fight it.

clarity_replaced_playhub_passages.old_body: Genealogy of the Holy War uses maps much larger than many earlier entries in the series. Castles, roads and groups of units form fronts that can require long movement, and capturing a position changes the flow of battle. Scale creates a political feeling: the player is not clearing one room or isolated fortress but crossing entire regions. Cavalry, formation and movement planning therefore matter more. Terrain is not only a tactical obstacle; it becomes a visible measure of the war being told. The work's method becomes visible in this balance. Fire Emblem: Genealogy of the Holy War makes map scale and castles a playable consequence rather than a statement and lets the audience understand its meaning through action.

reviewed_repeated_template_copyedits.original_body: The two-generation structure allows the game to make a narrative rupture unusual for the series at the time. After investing time, equipment and affection in the first army, the player must reinterpret the world through children and the consequences left by their parents. The rules remain recognizable, but their emotional meaning changes. An inherited weapon or transmitted trait functions as concrete memory. The genealogy system therefore makes the history of the war persist inside the numbers used to fight it. The consequence extends beyond one feature. Fire Emblem: Genealogy of the Holy War uses generational shift and memory to turn a concrete choice into rhythm, memory and behavior, making the system a recognizable part of the work's identity.

old_entry.title: Digital Anvil
old_entry.subtitle: Digital Anvil and the Ambition of Borderless Space
old_entry.summary: On April 8, 1996 a group made up largely of Origin Systems veterans founded Digital Anvil in Austin.
body: On April 8, 1996 a group made up largely of Origin Systems veterans founded Digital Anvil in Austin. The name already suggested an encounter between craft and technology, while Chris Roberts carried the experience of Wing Commander and an ambition to push games toward more continuous, spectacular space worlds. The studio lasted less than a decade, moving through investment, extremely ambitious projects, acquisition by Microsoft and eventual closure. During that time it released Starlancer, Freelancer and Brute Force, leaving behind a particularly useful case study in the relationship between vision and production capacity. Digital Anvil matters precisely because its story is not a triumphal march: it shows what happens when the scale of an idea meets money, hardware, time and organization.

Chris Roberts arrived at Digital Anvil after watching Origin grow around the success of Wing Commander. The new studio was formed with other veterans and an explicit desire to recover a more compact structure while still tackling technologically ambitious games and mixing videogames with cinematic language. The contradiction is productive but dangerous: a smaller team promises agility, while larger worlds require capital, tools and schedules that tend to expand the organization. Digital Anvil's founding already contains the problem that will define its history: how to retain creative control as technical ambition keeps growing.

Freelancer begins as the project meant to make the idea of a vast, continuous and active space tangible. Trade, combat, factions and movement between systems are meant to coexist in a universe that remains readable without the severity of harder simulators. Development, however, stretches out and demands more resources than expected. When Microsoft acquires Digital Anvil in 2000, the project is reduced in scope and Roberts leaves leadership. The 2003 game preserves the ambition of accessibility and freedom, but also records the cost of promises made at too large a scale. Freelancer therefore remains a useful example of how a vision can survive precisely through compromises that change its form.

In December 2000 Microsoft acquires Digital Anvil and folds the studio into its production system. Some projects are sold, others completed under the new structure; Freelancer is followed by Brute Force and other work while Roberts gradually exits the company. In 2005 staff are redeployed and in January 2006 the company is formally dissolved. Closure does not erase the expertise: employees and founders continue elsewhere, while Digital Anvil's experience remains part of the history of space games and Xbox production. Its legacy is therefore less a surviving brand than a network of ideas, people and lessons about project scale.
